utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and counsel. I want to express the gratitude of the Prosecution for the Chamber's indulgence on allowing a couple of extra hours. There were some logistical issues, and we are very grateful to all who have assisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's something that we think might become the pattern, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Logistical?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. Starting at 11.00, rather than 9.00 or...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If we could hold that for a 65 ter conference point, I'd be very grateful. Thank you. Actually, it was refreshing, but we appreciate the assistance on all sides. If the Chamber is ready, the Prosecution will announce the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. If you would. And while that witness is being brought in, we'll deal with a matter for the Defence. I understand you have a further expert, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Joining the Defence team today in the courtroom is Colonel -- General Radovan Radinovic. He is a Defence expert for command and control, which is precisely the area that General Zorc will be talking about today. The Defence has familiarised General Radinovic with all the aspects of our defence work, as we have done in the case of our previous expert witnesses. Therefore, we would like to ask for your leave for him to be present in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I ask, as I did with the last witness, Mr. Rodic, whether you have informed the general of the importance of the confidentiality aspects of being a witness in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have, indeed, Your Honour, fully, and General Radinovic agrees with all of these obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will certainly allow the presence of the general during the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution is calling its next witness, General Milovan Zorc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please take the card that's given to you now and make the affirmation that's printed i it on it. If you would read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please take the card that is given to you now and make the affirmation that is printed on it. If you would read the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could sit down now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we're ready, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we commence, I want to clarify that the witness will be addressing the Chamber in the Slovenian language, and there is a translation booth that has a special -- it will be translated into English but from Slovenian, so that the Chamber is aware. I believe this is the first time we have had that language used in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I assume it is being also translated into the other languages of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Would you be good enough to state your full name, date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: My name is Milovan Zorc. I was born on the 20th of August, 1935, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you state what your nationality, your ethnicity is, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: My nationality is Slovene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No. Currently I'm not employed. I am retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you retire, and from what position did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of January, 2003, as an advisor for defence issues to the president of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please indicate the name of the president of the Republic of Slovenia for whom you worked up to the time of your retirement.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout that time, the president of the Republic of Slovenia was Mr. Milan Kucan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your undertaking your position with President Kucan, what did you do professionally? Were you a professional member of the Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a professional officer of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you begin your career in the Armed Forces? If you could take us through a history, of course briefly, as there is much in your report, but I want to make sure the points that are important are emphasised.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I began my military career after the -- finishing, completing, the military academy in 1958. After that, I was commander of a squad, of a platoon. I was also assistant to the commander of a regiment and of a division, and the head of the republican staff of the TO of Slovenia, as well as also a deputy of the TO of the republic, and I was also a commander of the 4th army corps in Sarajevo up until 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, where is the military academy that you attended? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The military academy was in Belgrade. Also, all the other military schools that I attended and completed were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1979 to 1981, did you have a position at the University of Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. From 1979 until 1981, I was the head of the chair of defence studies at the University of Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your becoming the commanding officer -- the commander of the 4th army corps in Sarajevo, what was the rank that you held and what were your duties? Where were you immediately prior to becoming the commander of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I was the head of the republican staff of TO. I was the rank of colonel. And I also, after that, held the rank of a commander of a division in Sarajevo. And in 1986, I became major general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what division was it that you held the rank of [Microphone not activated] in Sarajevo? What division?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: It was the 4th ground division, infantry division, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you leave the forces, the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I left the active service in the Defence Forces of Yugoslavia on the 30th of June, 1991. It was at my own wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come about making your departure from the armed services? Was a request of any kind put in? If so, when?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. I left the active service at my own request, which the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. request was submitted in April 1991. And the reasons for those were the following: Up until 1991, for five years, I was living separately from my family, which was still living in Ljubljana. Secondly, in the active service of the Armed Forces, I see no prospects for me any more, and I also met the requirements for early retirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any resistance to your putting in your request for retirement or was it a smooth process?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No. No. I had no problems with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you actually leave the armed services? Were you to have left in July or was there a period of remaining at the disposition of?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: In fact, I left the military service on the 17th of May, 1991, because at my request, on the 6th of May, the Presidency of Yugoslavia took a decision on my request, and they issued an order that my service be terminated. And on the 17th of May, I transferred the functions to the corps commander and stopped being a military. Up until the 30th of June, I was in the status of being at the disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to a point where you actually left the military prior to the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. All this what occurred was prior to the conflicts in 1991, which began on the 27th of May -- correction, 27th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you go to work, or did you enter the services for president --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may just be permitted. It's something to do with the interpretation. The witness said, as far as I heard, on the 27th of June, he had the conflict in Slovenia in mind, which is not accurately reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Shall I repeat the question for you, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you go to work for or enter the services of President Kucan?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: In fact, I was invited to attend consultations the next day, on the 28th of June, and from then on, in form only, I was advising the Presidency concerning decisions they have to take on the military area. All this took place up until 19 October 1991, when I was also officially appointed as an advisor to -- for defence matters to the Presidency of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From June 1991 on, did you ever perform any further functions for the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No. After leaving the active military service, I performed no work whatsoever for any armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, turning now to some points in your report. Can you please identify or itemise the levels of command and control. What are the levels -- I think you made reference to three levels of command and control. What are they, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The command and control system in the Armed Forces of the former Yugoslavia was on the strategic operational, and tactical level. Each of these levels had one or more levels of command within that level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate what the operational group is in terms of a formation in the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia, former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: An operational group is a provisional, a temporary formation of the armed forces which, in its framework and the meaning of its mission, is of an operational nature. Therefore, the command of such an operational group is on an operational level, as -- similarly as in the regular army formations, is a ground, land corps in the military naval district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a commander of an operational group? Are there all the indicia of command and control in an operational group, starting with a commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Any unit or formation must have a commander and on a higher level also a command. Therefore, an operational group had to have a command which is headed by the commander of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do principles of command and control apply to an operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All principles of command and control are uniform for all the armed forces, which includes the operational group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether or not an operational group may in size reflect a corps-level formation or an army-level formation, does that change any aspect of command and control that applies to it? Does its size in that sense make any difference? Does command and control still apply?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The size of the formation or a unit of -- even of a temporary one, as is an operational group, does not influence the principles, the content of a command and control for that given unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the commander of the operational group the only commander who issues orders related to -- who issues orders related to the operations -- to the units of that operational group, operations related to the units. I hope I haven't confused that. But I'll repeat it if it helps. Is the commander of the operational group the only commander who issues orders related to the operations of the units of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia, there was the command principle. Any unit or formation had only one commanding officer, and also the operational group had only one commanding officer. So yes, the singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The expectation, is there the same expectation that when an -- I'm sorry. What is the expectation when an order is issued? What is the expectation of the commander who issues the order?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: When the officer in authority issues an order to a subordinate, it's not only his personal expectation, but it's also the legal expectation that that order is fully implemented, executed, without any discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The implementation of orders, what is the responsibility of the commanding officer to supervise the implementation of orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The responsibility of the commanding officer who issues a combat or other order to the subordinate unit is responsible fully for its implementation, and he must ensure that this order is then fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the order is not fully implemented, what is the responsibility of the commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The responsibility for an incomplete implementation of the order differs. If the subordinate had all the possibilities to implement the order, then the responsibility of the subordinate and the superior is total. But if the circumstances conflict, or limited possibilities of implementation, then this can be accepted as a part of the situation, and additional measures are then taken for the full implementation of the order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Must the commander, however, be made aware and accept -- does it go back to the commander, who must accept that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander must be informed, not only when but also how and with what effects the order has been implemented. And if it partly it had not been implemented [as interpreted], the reasons must be given for that partial implementation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reporting. What is the system by which commanders become informed of the activities of their subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Commanders at all levels are regularly informed about the actions of the subordinate units, about the situation in the units, and about the foreseen tasks for the units. This is ensured by regular and extraordinary reporting in battle. It can be battle reporting. In peacetime, it is daily reporting. Data -- daily regular reporting. And it refers to all important events taking place, and if there are some extraordinary events, then also extraordinary reporting is directed towards the commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do commanders have to keep themselves informed? Is there a continuous reporting system, particularly in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said, commanders must be, and they are responsible for setting up such a reporting system so that they can be informed fully Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about the situation in the subordinate units. This is done through regular reporting, interim reporting, from the front, or in the area where something important is happening. They can also send their officers from their staff to the subordinate unit where these subordinates then follow and report to the commander, and also through information they receive from other bodies, civilian bodies or some other neighbouring units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate how many levels below the reporting the commander expects to be kept directly informed of? Below and above.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The number of levels of subordinate units from which the -- he receives information and reports and precise data concerning the situation is two levels below. That's formally speaking. The commander receives information reports from the first level below, and it informs about what its subordinate levels and units are doing. In this way, the commander is informed about the two lower levels he is commanding. This is as far as formal reporting is concerned. However, his responsibility and interest to know what the situation is must be comprehensive and he must reach out to the very last soldier. This refers information concerning his units. In order to be able to judge the situation in his unit, each commanding officer must be informed about the broader, the general situation, namely, concerning two levels above. Thus, let us take, for example, the corps commander must be in detail informed what the other units, superior units in the district, military district, what the neighbouring units are doing. The first level, about the first level, he must be informed in detail. As the second higher level, the corps, he must be informed about the general situation in the armed forces and the objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is applicable also to operational group command and control aspect?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to any command whatsoever, also of the provisional groups, as is the case of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The obligation to be informed, would that also include the obligation to affirmatively seek out the information necessary to know what is taking place in zone of responsibility where the unit, the subordinate units, are found? In other words, is it a passive or is it an active function?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. It is the interest and the obligation of the commanding officer to know what the position and situation of his subordinate units is, in his zone of responsibility, is so important that he must not allow to passively wait to be the recipient of information. There is a compulsory system of reporting. He has intelligence bodies that -- he has other bodies in his command. And he cooperates with neighbouring units. In that way, he collates data, he cooperates with the civilian bodies in his zone, and of course there is also intelligence operations against the other side in case of hostilities. He must also activate them in order to be able to get as big as quantity as possible of relevant data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In combat, can the commanding officer, particularly, let's say, of a formation such as the operational group, wait to learn from the enemy side, the opposite side, about what that commanding officer's units have done perhaps in the way of use of weaponry or implementation of attacks, to be considered fully informed under command responsibility? Is that the means by which it is done?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: As I have already noted in the course of the previous question, in no case can the commanding officer, if an example is an operative group commanding officer, cannot be left waiting to be informed or to be informed by somebody else, not by his subordinate unit. When it comes to the activities of its own subordinate units, he cannot just simply wait for the information to come to him. He must be informed by his own units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the obligatory informing by his own units, can he, the commander, act or at least react to information concerning his troops' activities that comes from perhaps the other side or third parties, as an additional means of being informed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. The underlying problem in passing decisions is the quality of information and the reliability of information, and not just the source of information. The source could be within his own units, could be from the neighbouring units. Neighbouring units could be the source of information. It could be the public. Mass media could be the source of information or any other data coming from the population, et cetera. It is essential that the commanding officer assesses that the data is credible and this is enough grounds for taking action if action is needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Must the commander -- or is there an obligation to do that in a timely, responsible way?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: You mean in terms of his reaction?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Reaction, verification, assessment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Any decision should be taken in a time when it can still be efficient. Therefore, as a rule, as quickly as possible, or immediately, so as to be able also to take remedial reaction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Everyone has been provided with a binder of documents that were part of the footnotes of the report, and there would be some additional documents perhaps outside of that binder. The binder also may have -- may contain documents which had previously been exhibited, and we will inform the Chamber if referring to those documents what the previous exhibit number is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask to turn to the tab in the binder which contains tab 19, please. There are, I'm informed, Your Honours, some seven tabs which contain documents that are previously exhibited. I can -- we can discuss this, but it might be preferable to resubmit the entire binder, because it is footnotes, or I can do it individually so that there's no confusion whatsoever about the -- any exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to be in the pattern of tendering individual, having started the other way, there have been found to be inconveniences in that, I gather.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I am fine with either way. I want it so that the Chamber has the easiest way of accessing the -- I know some documents are with one number, then tab such-and-such. Mr. Hvalkov, Admiral Jokic's was a different -- I'm fine with going individually and just making sure that everything that was footnoted is given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we have tended to be guided by counsel's judgement as to which is to be the most convenient. Counsel's judgement is not necessarily always been correct, but it's hard for us to know at the beginning of a witness which is likely to prove in the end the most practical. What is essential, whichever system is followed, is that if a document is actually already an exhibit, that the record clearly reveal that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My preference is to individually do this. I think it's better practice for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think generally that has tended to be your practice. It's not necessarily been universal among the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask -- you have the versions in the English language as well as in the Serbo-Croatian language, and I'm going to ask you if you can indicate what that particular document is that is before you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, if I have the same document as you, it concerns the instructions of the federal secretary of defence concerning the use of the rules of the war law, and these are instructions that were adopted by virtue of a regulation of the Presidency of Yugoslavia as the commander-in-chief of the Yugoslav Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The English translation reads federal -- Federal Secretariat for National Defence. Regulations on the application of international laws of war in the Armed Forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you: Have you -- are you familiar with this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. particular document and these rules or regulations that are contained therein?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Article 20: "20. Personal responsibility for violations of the laws of war. Every individual - a member of the military or a civilian - shall be personally accountable for violations of the laws of war if he or she commits a violation himself or herself or orders one could be committed. Ignorance of the provisions of the laws of war do not exonerate the transgressors from responsibility." Is this a principle that has not only in this document been part of the rules, regulations, the doctrine of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia, but is it also in other areas of doctrine? Is it a fundamental principle that is found throughout various documents upon which commanders rely?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. We can indeed say that personal responsibility is part and parcel of relations within the Yugoslav Armed Forces, including also responsibility for the respect of orders, as well as compulsory orders such as this one and similar orders and instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Article 21, please. "Responsibility for the actions of subordinates. An officer shall be personally liable for violations of the laws of war if he knew or could have known that units subordinate to him or other units or individuals were planning the commission of such violations, and, at a time when it was still possible to prevent their commission, failed to take measures to prevent such violations. That officer shall also be held personally liable who, aware that violations of the laws of war have been committed, fails to institute disciplinary or criminal proceedings against the offender, or, if the instituting of proceedings does not fall within his jurisdiction, fails to report the violation to his superior officer." Reading further: "An officer shall be answerable as an accomplice or instigator if by failure to take action against his subordinates who violate the laws of war, he contributes to the repeated commission of such acts by units or individuals subordinated to him." This provision, can you indicate practically, in a practical manner, what this requires in combat for a commanding officer to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: While this particular provision, under the scope of this rule, has the intention, obviously, that the provisions in question should indeed be abided by in everyday practice, as well as the combat activities of the Yugoslav Armed Forces. And the people or institutions that are to guarantee this are institutions of command and control, the chain of command, from the very superior or commander-in-chief to the lowest level of commander. And it is stipulated thereby that all commanding officer should indeed take on board and adopt individual measures and do their utmost and the necessary so that the provisions of such an order be implemented in practice. Should anyone fail to do so, they do not in fact abide by the duties of command and control in accordance with the law and this order or these provisions, and that is a provision guaranteeing this. And then the last paragraph actually makes this responsibility of all officers, senior officers, even greater in case of failure on their part not to adopt measures and makes them actually co-responsible for any punishable or criminal acts carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come [Microphone not activated] in a short time to a discussion about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come in due course to a discussion about the nature of measures that are at the disposal of a commander. But a question to you, General, is: In addition to whatever may be provided by regulation or law, do there also exist measures for dealing with situations such as the ones we've just discussed, that arise purely from the authority of a commanding officer? Perhaps it might euphemistically be called de facto, but that arise from the authority of a commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, if what you have in mind is -- are the provisions of -- under Article 21, I must say that it is especially the second paragraph that deals with criminal responsibility of officers, senior officers, in the event where they violate or in fact are a violation of the rules of the law. And any commanding officers in this case are responsible for order, discipline, combat readiness, as well as the adequate activities, appropriate behaviour on the part of their forces. And it arises from the very function of commanding officer whereby they should see to it that the orders are indeed carried out in accordance with the law and regulations. Regulations say that it is indeed forbidden to commit a criminal act. So therefore, that arises from his very position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to Article --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 33 is the next provision I'd ask you to look at. The general heading of that section is "Criminal responsibility for war crimes and other serious violations of the laws of war." Looking at Article 33, is a non-exhaustive list. It is a list of war crimes and other serious violations, to include -- and then there are various things that are enumerated. If you look under section 5, which is on -- section 5, not Article 5, section 5 of Article 33, there is perhaps about halfway down, both opening fire at undefended places and non-military targets, deliberate bombardment of the civilian population. And lower down, close to the bottom, in the English translation, destruction of monuments of culture and of historic monuments and buildings and institutions with scientific, artistic, education or humanitarian goals. How are these categorised, General. What is the degree of seriousness of these violations that I have just addressed?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The acts perpetrated here in this guideline, this is operational guideline by the operational commander, includes all these violations of international law, so that commanding officers would not carry with them international treatise. And the significance of all this is that in all armed forces, including commanding officers, are informed in advance as to what is prohibited and what constitutes crime in Yugoslavia. All these activities mentioned here are also contained in the criminal law of Yugoslavia. The significance of this is very high, because it is a criminal act if perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whether -- are these criminal acts, whether or not there is a formal declaration of war, a state of imminent threat of war, or any other state? Are they criminal acts at all times?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: To my mind, it applies to any armed conflict, whether the state of war is declared or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will turn shortly to what the responsibility as to dealing with criminal behaviour is, what the commander's responsibility is. But I would ask also to take a look at Article 34, please. "Criminal offences against humanity and international law." And then it cites that: "In conformity with its international obligations, the SFRY has prescribed in the Criminal Code of the SFRY," chapter 11, criminal offences against humanity and international law, "that violations of the laws of war referred to in item 33 of these instructions constitute criminal offences and are punishable." And then they go on again to cite particular ones and the -- about the fourth one up cites: "Destruction of cultural and historic monuments." And war -- and further up, second from the top of the list: "War crime against the civilian populations." The -- can you just briefly at this point explain the interrelationship between the Criminal Code and then crimes that are -- of the SFRY and crimes that are enumerated in the laws of armed conflict, such as the one we are looking at now? Because they are referred to in Article 34. If you could maybe just help clarify or explain a little bit about the interrelationship.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Crimes against humanity in international law are contained here for information, so that military persons reading this guideline are aware Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what crimes in Yugoslavia are stipulated as criminal acts. All these criminal acts are contained in the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, thus becoming criminal acts in Yugoslavia. They have been introduced into the internal Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. And in view of the fact that these are criminal acts, if perpetrators are military perpetrators or civilian perpetrators, it is the military justice dealing with it, or military courts and military prosecutors. They deal with all criminal acts of military persons perpetrated against international law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at Article --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at Article 36: "Establishment of facts and provisions of violations of the laws of war. A Yugoslav officer who learns of violations of the laws of war shall order that the circumstances and facts surrounding the violation be investigated and the necessary evidence collected." The language there is "shall." What, then, is your view of the thoroughness, the energy with which a commanding officer, under circumstances that would be indicated in this article, act in order to fulfil the requirements of Article 36? Can you comment on how a commanding officer should conduct himself in order to fulfil this obligation of law?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Article 36 obviously stipulates yet again ways and means and who is supposed to carry out this particular guideline within the armed forces. And therefore, in command and control system, commanding officers shall use all the energy of their command so as to fulfil the requirements so that in case crimes occur, the perpetrators who are their subordinates will be court-martialled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 38, please: "Conducting criminal proceedings. The competent Yugoslav authorities shall conduct criminal proceedings against perpetrators of serious violations of the laws of war according to the provisions of the Law on Criminal Proceedings, the Law on the Military Prosecutor's Office, the Law on Military Courts, and the provisions of the regulations on the organisation and jurisdiction of military courts and proceedings before military courts during an imminent threat of war and a state of war." Then the provision concerning prisoners of war is not something I'm going to highlight at this point. As this -- because this provision exists as part of the regulation or law which governs commanders, must there be provision for these institutions to exist at all times or to be made -- if -- to be available? Must these institutions, such as the courts, military prosecutor's offices, must they be at the disposal of commanders in order to carry out their command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No. It seems to me that military courts and military prosecutor's offices must not be at disposal to commanding officers for fulfilling of their obligations concerning this particular provisions or rules and regulations. This particular --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think perhaps you misunderstood my question. Let me rephrase it. The obligations imposed by law on commanders require that certain matters be undertaken by them, by them, and perhaps through a different part of the process, military prosecutor's offices, courts - that are not part of the commander's jurisdiction - have to be used. Does the system, does the system for an efficient military require the existence and availability of these institutions in order for the provisions of this article to work? Is my question clearer to you? If not, I'll give you a specific example.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Before you give me a specific example, it seems to me that I have understood the question even before. For my introduction, I noted that military justice, by and large, is independent. It is not part and parcel of commanding of military units. The very fact that military commanding officers on all levels must inform military prosecutor's office in case of perpetration of a crime against international humanitarian law, or any crime, for that matter, that such a fact of crime does exist, to my mind, if there is or there isn't -- if the military justice exists or doesn't exist, it is not the matter of military commanders. It is the matter of the state, as such. Therefore, it seems to me that military commanders can always provide for the fact on ostensible perpetration of a crime is forwarded to military prosecutor's office at any level available. So what at a later stage the justice does, it no longer falls within the competencies or the mandate of military commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If, for example, a military court or other institution in the process described here is not available in a location close to where the commander and his units are situated, does that excuse the commander from carrying out his obligations with respect to the investigation and what we've just discussed? Perhaps part two of that question is: Would the existence of courts elsewhere compensate for that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. The availability of military justice body and military prosecutor's office, in the first place, in the vicinity or in the zone of individual commander and their unit is not essential. If there are some reasons the availability of military prosecutor's office or unit of military prosecutor's office is not actually available on the level of a division corps, an individual military zone, then it is available at a higher level, and the commander may or shall or must, when it comes to the information of a perpetrated crime, ostensibly perpetrated crime, the commander must inform his superior as far as the secretariat of military defence [as interpreted], and as regards the internal organisational structure of military prosecution, they are the ones who have to pinpoint which prosecution is going to deal with a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General Zorc, there is a use of the term "discipline" which may have a specific meaning, or let's say discipline or disciplinary. I want to make sure that when we use certain terms, we understand each other. The way of dealing with various offences in the armed forces, does it depend on whether an offence is considered disciplinary or criminal? Does the categorisation of an offence as disciplinary or criminal have a bearing on how it is -- how its treatment, how it's processed in the military system of the forces of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The term "discipline" refers to military discipline. Military discipline, disciplinary offences, mistakes, measures, require -- refer to the violations of military relations and order in the military force, Armed Forces of Yugoslavia. And these questions do not imply criminal proceedings or the Yugoslav terminology in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does cover criminal proceedings in Yugoslav terminology? How is the distinction made between what you have just described as disciplinary offences and criminal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, prosecution of perpetrators of crimes is a part of the state order, and it's not a part of the military system. It's the prosecution of criminal acts. And which are described and foreseen in the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia and which are -- a special procedure is foreseen for the prosecution of these criminal acts in the courts, be it military or civilian, in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when these criminal acts are found to have been committed by persons in the armed services, is there a difference in the way they are dealt with by the commanding officers? In other words -- perhaps you could give us an example of a disciplinary offence, as you just referred to, and then I'll ask you in a moment to give us an example of a criminal offence, and how they might be treated by commanding personnel, commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Violations of military discipline are foreseen in the Law on Military Service, and there it specifies violations of military discipline, military relations. And if they are less important, less significant, they are disciplinary mistakes. If they're more serious, they are disciplinary offences. And how they are treated: They -- we have process rules which are specified in that law, and they apply for internal military relations. On the other hand, criminal offences, which are then prosecuted by military courts, are prosecuted in line with the code, Criminal Code, and the law of procedure. It's possible that a single act may be a criminal act and a violation of military discipline. In that case, the violation is treated as a criminal act by the military court. But in exceptional cases, disciplinary measures may also be taken. So in certain cases, if it's a criminal act, it can also involve the violation of discipline, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

Perhaps from your own experience you can give an example, and how it is inquired into or looked at, how it comes to the attention of the commanding officer and what is happening after that, the process?

Despite all the best efforts of our interpreters to put the message across into English and then back from English into B/C/S, or Slovene, the substance of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. translation or the interpretation is quite generalised, imprecise, in certain aspects, and even occasionally inaccurate. This would naturally call for constant interventions on the part of the Defence team and carefully examining the transcript in relation to what the witness today has said. The Trial Chamber and this Tribunal respect everyone's right to choose their own language in addressing the Trial Chamber, despite which, in this case, the Defence would like to propose the following, with the witness's content: For the witness to speak B/C/S, if he can, if he's willing to, because that would make the whole process of interpretation a lot simpler and the result would probably also be a more accurate transcript. Therefore, I would like to have this matter looked into, whether there is a possibility to do something like that, especially given the fact that most of the tabs, most of the documents in the binder, are in B/C/S, the original texts. First he reads the B/C/S, then the Slovene version, and then from Slovene it's being interpreted into English, and then from Slovene backtranslated into B/C/S. Therefore, we have almost four simultaneous interpretations of one and the same substance. Some of that substance is lost along the way. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Clearly, Mr. Petrovic, every process of interpretation has the potential to introduce some inaccuracy on a particular matter. Occasionally, that may be material. It would not be the view of the Chamber that a witness should be required to speak in a language other than their first language. It is for a witness to indicate the language in which they are most at ease to give their evidence. Therefore, the Chamber would not require or direct the witness to give evidence in any language other than his own language. If it is his free wish to give his evidence in another language of the Tribunal other than his own language, he may do so, but, as I understand it, he has chosen to give his evidence in the Slovene language. That being so, and if that continues to be his position, we must, as we have throughout the trial, deal with any material discrepancies in the translation by correction as they become apparent. That will slow the process a little, and we may not always have a perfect translation, because, in particular, of the multiple steps through which the process is occurring. But it is nevertheless the best we can manage, and experience shows that it generally proves adequate. Ms. Somers, I leave it to you. You have dealt with the witness. utterances.text: General, just before the lunch break, we began -- I asked you a question about various types of punishment, basically. Now, can you confirm that punishment is divided into criminal and disciplinary?

utterances.text: Yes. These are two different matters. Criminal acts, and they're defined and are the same for all citizens of a state, while the disciplinary violations, and they are also measures, countermeasures, are foreseen for the military, because it is something internal to the military. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry. Are disciplinary violations handled before the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: You said before?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I have to explain this. Military -- violations of military disciplines, as I have said, can be of a milder nature or a more serious nature. The responsibility of a military for violations -- and it's left to the commanders and superior commanders. Violations -- milder violations carried out by the officers or non-comms are left to their commanders and the superiors. Only more serious violations of military discipline carried out by non-comms and officers are a matter for the disciplinary -- military disciplinary court.

He's talking about the soldier as a member of the armed forces. To put it in the simplest possible way, at the lowest possible level.
