utterances.text: May the witness once again be reminded to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, military discipline is violated by the military. They can be soldiers or superior officers with a rank. They can be non-commissioned officers or officers. These are two categories. It means soldiers and officers. Now, for violations of military discipline, milder ones, for both structures, their Superior Command is responsible, that is, for the soldiers and the officers or non-commissioned officers. For more serious, more severe violations, disciplinary violations, is also responsible their superior officers, but for the officers and non-comms, the commander cannot deal with their serious violations, and for that, the military disciplinary court is responsible. The responsibility and the process for the dealing with serious offences of disciplinary offences, it's more serious because they are therefore treated and processed in front of the disciplinary military court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the military disciplinary court located?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: They are at the level of certain commands. It can be the army command or of an army area. And in times of war, they are foreseen also at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they are nearer to the commander, where the commander is physically located? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. They are institutions close to the commands and also the judges. They are also elected from the various -- judges are elected from the ranks of officers, so it is closer, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who establishes -- who sets up military district -- I'm sorry- military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: They are established by the command structure from the federal secretary and the commanders of the military districts. So they are appointed by military commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we are dealing with criminal violations, serious criminal violations, criminal violations, now, are these handled by a different organ called a military court?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: As I've explained, all criminal acts perpetrated by the military persons are treated by the military justice, namely, military courts, military prosecutors of the former Yugoslavia. And they are not within the system of command and control. They are independent justice institutions in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is a military court generally found in a military district in terms of its location, its placement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You seem to be assuming it has a physical location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can a military court be convened or placed within a military district? Tell us about the military courts. What -- where are they generally? How are they set up? Who establishes them? Who runs them?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Military courts and prosecutors are established by law, which were adopted by the Assembly of the Parliament. The setting up of military courts and of the prosecution, and the appointment of the judges and prosecutors, was in the competence of the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of Yugoslavia. The courts were organised in a way that the courts, at the first level, and the supreme military court. The first-level courts covered the entire territory of Yugoslavia and were formed for a certain part of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. These were in a different location, namely, in the cities where also higher commands were located, the commands of the armies or the military districts. Therefore, they were formed for certain territories, and all the criminal acts perpetrated by the military were then treated and processed by the military court for that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is -- who is the -- what is the organ or who is the person to whom criminal violations are referred within this military court system? Does there exist a military prosecution, a military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain the role of that military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can. I've mentioned in my previous answer. I spoke about military courts and the military prosecution. Military prosecutor's office were founded in a similar fashion as the military courts. At the first level, they were in the same premises, the same location as the first-level military courts. And they have the role of investigating crimes as in civilian life. And if there is an information concerning a certain possible criminal act, information coming from anybody, but usually it comes from the organs of the military police, the security organs of the armed forces, or individual superior officers of this alleged -- the information concerning a criminal act is then sent -- this information is sent to the public -- to the military prosecutor. This information is then sent to the prosecutor, who then asks the investigating judge to investigate this alleged crime, and it is then the prosecutor who will judge whether he will prosecute or not. Here, from the point of view of military command and control, the role of the superior officers, the commanding officers, is very important. All citizens of Yugoslavia have the obligation to report the alleged criminal offences to the military police or the military prosecution. However, the superior officers, the commanding officers, had a greater responsibility concerning this sending of information. They were officers who have a higher responsibility concerning discipline, order, within their units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the witness kindly be reminded to slow down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I want to convey the request of the interpreters to try to speak more slowly so they can catch everything. Thank you. If I can ask you, General, now: You've given us an introduction to the system. Can you give examples, examples, of let's say what you called a mild violation occurring by a subordinate of a commander, and how that is handled and how -- and what types of punishment or -- yeah, what types of measures can be meted out by the commanding officer, the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: As I have already noted, if you speak in terms of disciplinary violations, that is, violations of military discipline, then, I repeat, violations of military discipline had been enlisted in the Law on Armed Forces Service and the same violations could be minor or more serious. If these violations were of a milder nature, minor violations, they were dealt with by superior military commanders. They had at their disposal measures, a number of measures, different sort of measures, for soldiers, stricter; for example, it would involve detention, prevention of exit, additional work, and similar. And for officers, military officers, they were of ethical nature, for minor violations. Disciplinary measures called warning, censure, and serious censure, were applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, can you give an example, an example. You were a commander [microphone not activated]. Just -- for example, failure to salute, failure to be on time, how would that be handled, if it were by a regular soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Perhaps failure to salute is an act that would not be liable for disciplinary liability, especially when applied to younger soldiers that are only being trained for military service. A better example to this effect would be arbitrary departure from unit, uncensured departure from the barracks, or unallowed absence of senior officer. So in what way a superior military commander would assess such an act depends on the situation. If the unit is performing a serious task, then any departure from the unit could constitute more serious violation of discipline. And of course the other way around is also true. The departure or absconding for a small period of time could be dealt with as a minor violation and is not sanctioned at all. However, if the person is an officer performing responsible duties in barracks, arbitrary departure or absence could be dealt with as a more serious violation of military discipline. This should not always be the case, depending on the tasks performed by the officer. If the officer commands a company, and if such an officer leaves, the entire company to wait for him, then, of course, it's a more serious violation than if an officer carrying out staff duty does not report for work. So it all depends on the post. Furthermore, if such an act, such as absence from work for several days without permission and without notification, occurs in relation to a senior officer, this could be dealt with as a more serious violation of military discipline. In such a case, their superior, on the level of the commander of regiment on higher level must initiate disciplinary investigation against such an officer. In order to carry out such a disciplinary investigation, one of the officers is mandated, and this particular officer must explore all the circumstances of the act committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you -- excuse me, general. The translation says an officer is mandated. Is that -- do I understand to mean appointed or designated? If you could perhaps clarify. It says: "In order to carry out such a disciplinary investigation, one of the officers is..." and the translation says "mandated." Can you perhaps explain what you mean. Are you referring to "appointed" or "designated"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Right. The responsible commanding officer identifies one of the commanding officers to carry out disciplinary investigation, "izvidjaj" in Serbo-Croat, and this is to explore all the circumstances of the case, and in the report to the superior commander should propose further measures, and these measures, or this particular report, can assess that the very violation was not of a serious nature. It can also identify that the violation was of a serious nature, thus suggesting the superior officer to provide for the perpetrator to face military court. In case the investigation has manifested that a minor violation of discipline was in question, then the matter is solved by the commanding officer himself by declaring a disciplinary measure, as I've already noted in one of my previous answers. If the perpetrator is put to military disciplinary court, then this court is dealing with entire case and also passing the judgement. Or passing the disciplinary sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we take a different example of a criminal violation, can you first of all indicate or confirm, based on some earlier testimony, what the obligation is of the commander, the superior commander, toward getting the information about the violation. Where does it have to go? How does a case -- how does a matter get to the military court? Give us the path.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Hence violations occur more or less in military units and military life. Criminal offences also occur within the framework of armed forces within military units and military barracks, but also beyond, in civil life, because military persons could commit crime offences of other sort, not only against armed forces. If this violation or assumed or ostensible criminal offence is assessed as potential criminal offence, then military senior officers might provide for this charge to come before the military prosecutor. When -- or until the military investigating judge does not take over this procedure into their own hands, the military senior officers must provide for the protection of potential evidence and for detention of the potential perpetrator if they have control over him or her. When the military investigating judge takes over the compilation on further data concerning the potential criminal offence, the responsibility of military senior officers comes to an end. From here onwards, the military investigating judge is carrying out all other measures, with the help of military police bodies and, on his requirement, also with the assistance of bodies of military command or military commanders, and then the military investigating judge then passes on his report to the military prosecutor that then takes decision on investigation. From here on, the criminal proceedings start, and it seems to me that I don't have to elaborate on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned military police. What is the role of military police in the -- in this process involving criminal violations?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Military police is vested with different tasks and functions. One of them is also criminal prosecution, that is, cooperation in criminal prosecution of perpetrators of criminal offences. In this particular function, this criminal-legal function, the military police bodies are carrying out the same tasks as any other police bodies are, including civilian police bodies. They are both liable and mandated to gather data to protect possible traces, evidences, to detain potential perpetrators, to gather other data, and also to detain the suspect, that is, potential perpetrator, until the investigating judge does otherwise. So military police is carrying out the well-known tasks in the field of criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the obligation, the responsibility of a commander to ensure that the information gets to the military prosecutor either on his own or through the military police or through some appropriate method in the system? What is that obligation?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I have already explained that. The obligation to report assumed criminal offence to the military prosecutor is one addressed with all the population and with all citizens. Commanders of the armed forces have a responsibility which is even greater to report on a criminal offence that falls within their scope. And information about an assumed criminal act in fact can come from any member of the armed forces or a civilian person to the military prosecution. It may come via or through commanders of the armed forces. They can also in fact provide information about this. However, as a rule, this is in fact carried out -- is carried out normally by the military police. Because when there is an offence or an assumed criminal act that has been committed, the superior officers call the military police. Once the military police has been notified, automatically the military prosecutor, especially the investigating judge, are also informed and notified, and it is then up to them to take further action. Superior officers, when I'm talking about the responsibility of the senior officers to report on criminal acts, that is also a responsibility of all superior officers. Let me give you an example. If this notification was, for instance, made by the commander from the battalion, for instance, from a company, there is no more need for anybody else to do it. If, for instance, the commander of the company failed to do so for lack of contact, for being in combat action and the like, he or she reports it to his superiors, and it is the superior officer that will do it, be it commander of the brigade, battalion, and the like. Whatever commander in the chain of command can actually report on it, whereas it is the responsibility of all commanders to report it. Once this is done, the function concerning this area ceases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the responsibility, if I understand it, is to ensure, to ensure, that the information is reported to the prosecutor, whether it's through the military police or whatever, but make sure -- to ensure that it is reported; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, where was the military court that would, in the autumn of 1991, have handled matters concerning Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, for the 9th military maritime district, that is indeed the Dubrovnik district, well, that was the responsibility of Split, of the Split district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If for any reason the military court --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an interpretation error. Military naval district in Split. That's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you distinguish between maritime and naval? That's what's recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. This is what my objection refers to. Page 46, the last line, line 25. [In English] [Previous translation continues]... of the Split district. [Interpretation] That's where the error is and how it should read is "military naval district" instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is said earlier in the sentence. I don't think it can be understood in any other way. But thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies, but I must step in and point this out, because it's absolutely substantial. In the very same sentence, the witness says the 9th military naval sector, the Dubrovnik area is in relation to that, which is under the competence of the military naval district in Split. That's the essence of that sentence. As far as I know, it's a reference to the 9th VPS, military naval sector, when it's about Dubrovnik. And this is the responsibility of the military naval district in Split, or rather, the headquarters. This is the substance of what the witness said, and I believe we can ask him to have this confirmed, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I don't read the answer, lines 23 to 25, as saying anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if that is the case, then indeed we don't seem to have a problem. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I inquire of the witness on that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, I think that I have to correct this, because I did not say that the 9th military maritime sector was within the competence of the military maritime district. What I said was that the competence of the military court in Split, in the area covered by the 9th military maritime sector. So what happened in the area of Dubrovnik is within the territorial competence of the military court in Split, and not of the district, because that is the military command, whereas here we are speaking about the judicial system, the military judicial system, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having asked you about the military court that would have had jurisdiction over matters in the Dubrovnik area and your response that you believe it was in Split, if for any reason that particular court and the personnel that would normally be attached to it were not available, where could a matter be held that would normally be held in Split? Which military court - or is there a choice - could handle it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, should it happen, for any reason, that the bodies of the military prosecution and the first-instance military court were unable, physically, to perform their duties, their tasks, then it would be the competence of the superior of the higher military court and military prosecution to determine what other prosecution or court would look into that matter. And the military commanders obviously cannot decide on such matters. And it is in the interest of the military commander to provide information about such possible criminal acts and that they should reach military prosecution, not necessarily some determined prosecutor's office. If one is not available, then it is decided which instance, other instance it should be referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "other instance," are you referring to which other location or jurisdiction, which other military court it would be referred to? I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And this is in the chain of command in this system of military courts and military prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give some locations where there were military courts during that time period?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, it is a bit difficult to enumerate them all, but I know that there was a prosecutor's office, military prosecutor's office in Ljubljana later on and also before in Zagreb. There was also both a court and prosecution in Sarajevo, where I was active, in Split as well, and also in other garrisons where they had superior commands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The unavailability or would the possible unavailability of one military court, let us say in Split, be any -- would it excuse a commander from his obligation to ensure that information about criminal offences nonetheless got passed up to a military court somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No. It would not exonerate that person from the duty to do so. As I have explained, if the military prosecutor's office does not exist in an area because there is combat, ongoing combat, or for some other reason, then it is the chain of command that in fact is respected, and the information should be provided by the next commander at the adequate level. And if at the first instance such a court is not operational, then we go up, further up the chain of command and up to the secretariat of defence, and thus in fact competence or authority is vested into some other military court of the first instance. And the same goes also for the military prosecution, prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies for interrupting. However, this last passage of the transcript, if possible, may we please have the answer to that particular question again, slowly. As far as I'm able to understand the language that the witness is speaking, the substance of what he said is not reflected in this particular interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to -- are you able, General, to take a look on your screen and see if it is correctly translated? It would be line 24 of page 49.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: I'm looking. I think that it corresponds to what I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, why is discipline, the concept of discipline, important in military organisational life?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The army or military organisation is a specific institution, and its purpose is, it is also equipped, designed for, equipped, as well as trained, for the use of force. That means that it is a very sensitive organisation in a country. And availing of a power that the armed forces avail of cause for a very solid internal set-up or internal organisation, as well as a very solid internal control. And this organisation and this control is ensured by the system of command and control, which also ensures the respect of specifically prescribed standards of behaviour by the military. And the military relations are determined or -- are determined by single officers, by this duty to issue orders, and also the fact that all subordinates have to strictly abide or respect and carry out the orders, while respecting very clearly all provisions of the military order and discipline. That is, therefore, a system of internal military relations, of internal military discipline, whose purpose is to guarantee that any senior officer in the chain of command, as well as also the state leadership, can trust its armed forces; namely, that their power will not be misused, abused. And these are the reasons, therefore, controlling, being in total command of all military is a reason that -- for which, of course, a very strict internal organisation and discipline are required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the enforcement of orders by a commanding officer critical -- the enforcement and implementation of orders, is it critical to maintaining the system of discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is essential for maintaining the military organisation, as well as ensuring the functioning of the system of command and control. Issuing -- implementing orders without a right to complaint actually is part and parcel, an essential part and parcel of the military organisation in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask to have Exhibit P198 put before the witness, please. It is chapter 20 of the Criminal Code - sorry - of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, Armed Forces. Sorry. Strike Armed Forces. It is the Criminal Code of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In chapter 20, if you would look at Article 201. Do you see it, General? Article 201 of chapter 20. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The overall chapter heading is "Criminal acts against the Armed Forces of the SFRY." Specifically, failure or refusal to carry out an order, Article 201: "1. If a member of the armed forces fails or refuses to carry out an order of a superior officer which is related to the service, and if this has serious detrimental consequences for the service, or if the service was seriously jeopardised, he shall receive a prison sentence of three months to five years. "2. If an act as described in paragraph 1 of this article incurs serious consequences for the service, the perpetrator shall receive a prison sentence of one two ten years. "3. If a member of the armed forces fails, through negligence, to carry out the order of a superior officer, as described in paragraph 1 of this article, he shall receive a prison sentence of up to one year." The seriousness -- would you agree that the -- that there is a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the act of carrying out an order, per se, or the failure to carry out an order per se, is one that has, in general, very serious consequences?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, yes, because this violates the very basis of the military organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the obligation of the commander to ensure that discipline is maintained, that orders are implemented, would there be a compromise in command and control if that commander did not carry out his obligations? Would the compromise -- would the failure to ensure discipline compromise the command and control of the superior officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No doubt, yes. Of course, if the subordinate does not carry out a single order, it is a very serious matter for the system of command and control and for controlling of the subordinate unit. If the subordinate does this several times and fails to carry out a number of orders, or if a number of subordinates do the same, then this constitutes an extremely serious matter, an extremely serious problem for a military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the signal sent to other persons in the unit if an order is given, it is not implemented, and there is no either discipline or inquiry or action taken as a result of the failure to implement the order?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Signal that is sent through the failure to act by the superiors by the failure to carry out orders to other members of military units would be very negative. The subordinates must feel that the requirements of the superiors and the requirements of military relationships and military organisation and regulations are serious and that the violations of these military relationships be tolerated. These must not be tolerated, because if this is so, then this might bring about disintegration of military organisational structure. If I add: The general prevention could be even more important than the individual one in a specific case in a military organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, in your view, is the effect of failure to enforce or to impose discipline for failure to enforcing -- to enforce orders, what is the effect on the -- what I might call the climate or the tone of the command?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: As I have already noted, if, against violation of military discipline, no measures are taken, or if nothing is done against a military person failing to carry out a military order, this can bring about the violation of military order, military discipline or disintegration of the organisational structure. It can bring about the situation when senior officers can no longer control their subordinate military units. The implications might be extremely negative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there exists a series of orders or directives from Superior Command not to shell or attack a particular site which is protected under international law, international humanitarian law, and the order is violated, it is not complied with, and damage is worked, there is damage that results, maybe in a -- damage to objects or to human beings, and there is no investigation - and I use the term in the sense of gathering information - as to the circumstances, what is the effect of those orders or directives?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: If I understand well, you aim at failure to carry out military orders and failure of superior commanders against -- to take measures against those that haven't carried out orders in military circumstances. In this context, I can only note that in such circumstances, the potential disintegration of military discipline and the inefficiency of military command and control is even more accentuated. The significance of such an act in war circumstances is much more significant than in peaceful circumstances. And therefore, the consequences of such a so-called tolerance could be disastrous in terms of controlling of military units, that in such circumstances can even more expand illegal operations within the framework of their units and on the territory they are located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the same orders or directives which are rooted -- which may be rooted in international humanitarian law are subsequently violated and there is no investigation again in the sense of gathering information about the incident by superior officers, what is the implication further for the value of the orders?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, the situation is the same as when it goes for military organisation. In case a violation of international humanitarian law or violation of rules and regulations by the federal secretary so as to respect international humanitarian law in wartime circumstances, this all in turn constitutes the significant lowering of respect of command and control on the part of low-ranking officers. This implies that such illegal acts could be further expanded, meaning that a greater number of members of armed officers -- armed forces officers could carry out more criminal offences for wartime, even though this would have to be discontinued and put an end to, and therefore, to my mind, the implications could be really disastrous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if, and if, other officers or other members of the armed forces were to carry out more offences during time of conflict, as you just referred, given the failure to enforce previous orders which resulted in these consequences, what, in your view, would those -- the other group, the further group, expect to happen to them if they violated the order? If it had not been punished once, twice, what is the expectation of any disciplinary or -- yeah, disciplinary in the sense of criminal system involvement? What do you -- how do you view that?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: If I understand well your question, I might note that failure to act already against the first violation of military discipline, or violation of military order, or lack of respect of military rules and regulations, the very first violation that has not been sanctioned can give an impression to other members of armed forces, or privates, or common troops, that we cannot expect to understand the rules and regulations of international humanitarian law or internal rules and regulations that military officers are to carry out, these people, in turn, could get a feeling that carrying out of offences, a violation of international humanitarian law is not ruled out, is not illegal, or is even tolerated, or even sanctioned, even allowed. Of course this impression is false or wrong, but it can occur if we fail to take measures against the first violation of orders. And consequences and implications might be further sprawl of illegal offences on part of members of armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the situation discussed where, despite the legal prohibition and orders affirming the prohibition against attacking certain protected sites, if, despite that, there is a -- you learn, as a commanding officer, that there is a violation, what do you do -- what would you do, under -- first of all, would you view that as a crime, the actual act of attacking, for example, a cultural monument? Is that a crime, a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Any type of information, an information about acts carried out by subordinate units, anything that could be in fact seen as a criminal act, is something that any commander should take very seriously and deal with very seriously. And in accordance with the rules, with the previously mentioned rules, such a commander should undertake everything in his power to establish the facts, the state of affairs, and once he does so, to then notify the military prosecutor in case he deems that this could be assessed as a criminal act. And if this criminal offence is conspicuous enough so that any, for instance, superior officer can justifiably say that this is indeed what happened, then what one can expect from subordinate officers, and all superiors expect from all commanders, namely, that they would in fact become involved personally, and personally would make it their personal commitment to prevent any future such acts, to put an end to it as soon as possible, if necessary, through personal intervention of commanders at ever-higher levels, so as to arrive at a moment when it is possible to prevent it. Whereas, of course, criminal measures, this is something that will be up to the criminal -- to the court.

utterances.text: Also, General, I'm sorry that I had to take a moment and do some logistical matters. Did you have a look at that order as well during your proofing session? It is not in front of you, General. It is not in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: No, I don't have it in front of me. But yes, the proposed order of the operational -- of the operational group, I did see it yesterday. Yes, I glanced through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's about interpretation again, page 66 [as interpreted], lines 18 and 19. And what the witness actually said is that it precedes the decision made by the 2nd Operational Group. Therefore, if we can please clarify this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you didn't mean page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I mean page 64. You are quite right. My apologies.

utterances.text: Ms. Somers, there's something there for you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, the question was whether or not there was -- there were elements of the first order that were reflected as well in the second -- in what was the order by -- order or proposal by Jevrem Cokic. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your response?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Concerning the -- general activities in the -- Dubrovnik and the JNA. I did not ask anything in particular about the 2nd Operational Group. That was not part of my question.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The document that you had shown me was a proposed decision on the use of the force of the 2nd Operational Group, and that all referred to September 1991. And what I have said was it was a proposed decision on the use and that this was the decision which preceded the use and the introduction of the operations of this group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to the questioning about violations of orders. I give you a scenario, and I would ask, please, that you listen very carefully to what I -- what my question is. An order to cease fire is in existence, has been issued. A member of an operational group, allegedly on his own initiative, undertakes to violate that order, undertakes to open fire in the face of a cease-fire in place. What would you view as the appropriate response of the superior officers concerning that violation of the order to cease fire?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, the violation of an order is, per se, negative and it should be sanctioned. What should the superior officer do in this situation will depend on whether this violation lasts so long that he has to get involved and stop it, or was the violation so brief that he can only act post-festum. Therefore, if it -- the violation lasts for a certain period of time, the superior commanders must get involved in order to stop, put a stop to this violation. Regardless whether they succeed or the violation is stopped, they must treat this violation and sanction this violation and adopt measures in order to avoid a repetition of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have -- we can break this into a second part. You have indicated that they must act to stop the violation. You have indicated that the duration of the violation is a factor into what they should do. Let us give the scenario in which the violation of a cease-fire order has the effect of a major, major outbreak of fire from the other side, with the result that there is now engagement by both sides. It lasts over a period of hours. Among the objects affected or targeted are protected areas, protected by international humanitarian law, as well as injuries to civilians protected by international humanitarian law. What would be the appropriate response of the commander upon realisation that it is not stopping quickly?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The violation of a cease-fire caused by one side, as a rule, gives rise to a response of the other side, and that's a rule of action. The other side cannot just wait and be a victim of the attack, irrespective of a cease-fire. How to stop such a conflict caused by a single violation, when both sides insist they didn't begin it, it's very difficult to stop such an attack, particularly a one-sided effort to stop it. But if you have such a battle position that it's clear that one side can stop, one-sidedly such a conflict caused by the initial violation and he withdraws, then such -- this can be done. And the superior officers can order this and withdraw the forces from the fire of the other side. But if they're in such a position where they cannot withdraw, then both sides, with the assistance of a third party or through mutual cooperation on a higher level, should simultaneously stop firing at each other. So this is a rather complex situation, but it's rather frequent when cease-fire violations occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the opening of fire, as I referred to earlier, by -- on the initiative of a unit, an operational group, if the opening of fire is contrary to a strategic goal, a cease-fire which is part of a greater strategic goal, what is the obligation, or what would be the appropriate response of the superior commanders to ensure that that strategic goal is met, this goal having been interfered with by the outbreak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can my colleague please say precisely which superior officers she has in mind, which level. First level, second level, third, fifth level? I think she should specify when she asks a question like this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The highest commanding officer in the operational unit. What is the obligation of the highest commanding officer in the operational group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean the commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The highest -- the commanding officer which is the highest level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the appropriate response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Commander, not commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I do this all the time. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are talking about abstract ideas and tasks that we must tackle. Therefore, may we have this explained clearly first. There is the battalion level, the battalion has its own Superior Command, which is the corps command, or the VPS command. And then the VPS command has its own Superior Command above them, as the OTP claim, the operational group. It is in that context that we should hear answers from the witness. It should be made perfectly clear which roles in which specific situations are implied by the question. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I leave it to you to formulate your question. If it isn't right, it won't be much use to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would, if I may, just respond to this particular point that I am specific about the operational group commander, and that is the thrust of my question. I deem everything else right now irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know about the appropriate response from the operational group commander as to the events that have flowed from the violation of a cease-fire order of one of his subordinate commanders, by one of his subordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: If you ask me about the situation which existed around Dubrovnik when you had the violation of a cease-fire, from the military point of view, I should state that we should see who took the initiative and who was attacking and who was defending. The attacker has the opportunity of withdrawing from the attack, and the defender not. The 2nd Operational Group was performing -- carrying on operation. And it was -- he was running the operational group commander. And the commanders of VPS and the commanders of the brigades and of the battalion. They all had their share of responsibility. So you said that it depends on the strategic interest, what is to be done in case of a violation of a cease-fire. I must say that first we have to see what is the strategic interest. Was it for the operational group commander to maintain the blockade of Dubrovnik, or was his primary interest the prevention or stopping this violation of cease-fire? What was more important for him? I cannot assess that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me give you a scenario where the strategic goal is to have a cease-fire in effect, and I will add a dimension for you, that the commander one level down from the operations group commander has given an order that fire cease. It has not been obeyed. It has not been obeyed. It appears not to be obeyed. What is the appropriate response of the operations group commander under those circumstances? If you can be very specific and brief, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: In such a concrete case, if a cease-fire has been imposed, it's also in the interest of the two sides to maintain it. The commander whose side has committed this violation should have intervened if he had the opportunity. If he had the initiative, the place, he could do so to stop the other side, but also withdraw his units to another place so that the other side wouldn't have the other -- the targets and would stop its fire, and the cease-fire would be in place again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's an interpretation problem yet again. Page 71, line 1. [In English] [Previous translation continues...] side has committed this violation. [Interpretation] The witness used the word "commander" and then the word "unit" or "enota," in Slovene. I think that means "unit." The commander, therefore, whose unit committed the violation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you like to clarify, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My counsel opposite has asked what particular word -- let's see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I asked you and you answered, you said: "[And] in such a concrete case, if a cease-fire has been imposed, it's also in the interest of the two sides to maintain it." Then the transcript says: "The commander whose side has committed this violation should have intervened if he had the opportunity." Did you intend, if I understood correctly, to use the term -- was it -- if I understood correctly, Your Honour "commander"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, no. Whose unit or whose side has committed this violation. I'm not sure what it is the witness wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unit. Unit. Unit. Whose subordinate unit participants in the violation of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had mentioned the commander whose side has committed this violation should have intervened. How should the commander whose side committed the violation, how should he have intervened? Can you tell us concretely what type of intervention you had in mind, possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the question should read: Whose subordinate unit has committed the violation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. The subordinate unit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: At present, I can't define what I would do myself, how I would stop the violation of the cease-fire. Of course, there are many possibilities. The first, the easiest is via means of communication to issue an order to the subordinates down to the perpetrators of the violations, of the shelling, to stop that action immediately. Of course, if it's possible, he can also order to -- order to stop the shelling and to withdraw from that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If such orders are given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry. I was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- pause for the transcript. He may not have finished his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course, the commander also can and must also more efficiently, if the issuing orders -- the issued orders do not reach the subordinate or if they're not effective. And in that case, send a deputy or somebody else on the location, or somebody else, or that he personally issue orders, or even go personally to that unit, and there, stop directly the shelling, of course, if he decides -- so decides or if he can order the withdrawal of the unit. If all that isn't feasible, then, at a higher level, they meet and both sides decide on a new cease-fire. Both sides can then decide to stop this violation of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this violation of the cease-fire is occurring, I put to you that areas of historic or cultural interest protected by international humanitarian law are being shelled by units under the command of the operational group. As time goes by, more and more damage is occurring. Efforts to bring the firing to a halt, through the intervention of subordinate officers, but high-ranking subordinate officers, have failed. What is the appropriate response for the operational group commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, in the event -- we have a situation where one side is shelling the protected monuments, cultural monuments and so on -- in such a case a cease-fire to stop fire is an obligation that the subordinate officer should be able to obtain, regardless of the fact that the other side also is involved in fire. Because this shelling is unauthorised even not if this is fire on both sides. If the first or the second order are not successful, then there is no other -- in fact, other solution than for the commanding officer to be there even personally so as to put an end to it. There is no other possibility. Therefore, on the site, on the site of the battle, of the fire itself. So that in fact through his intervention, this be stopped on the spot. Here, of course, I'm speaking about the operational -- of operational activity, in fact, within the area of such activities and within a short period of time. Another matter is indeed how, later on, responsibility of those having taken part in the violation of cease-fire will be raised and in this illegal attacks on protected areas and monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated an appropriate response may be for the commander himself to go to the area. Can you comment about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, which commander are we talking about? Please, let's clarify. Which commander do we have in mind here? Battalion commander, brigade commander, corps commander, or the commander of the operational group, an army-level unit? Please let us have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have been asking, General, to clarify about the operational commander, the commander of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the commander you had in mind who should personally intervene and if all other measures fail to go?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: By all means, this is a responsibility to be borne by all commanders in the chain of command, from the top to the bottom, including also the infantry, battery, for instance, the infantry company, all of them have this responsibility. And if all the lower levels do not do it, then obviously up to the very highest level, and that is in that case, in that particular case, the commander of the operational group. And this situation is already very problematic; namely, that he is not capable of stopping the problem through the other levels and that he has to become involved personally. However, it cannot be excluded, and in the extreme case, this is something he should do as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is an appropriate response -- would an appropriate response include removal or physical removal from the scene of the offending lower-level commander, let us say a battalion commander for the sake of argument, who continues actively to be involved in attacks?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Possibly. But this is not a formal removal of a commander from the commanding post, but possibly, for instance, the superior officer in some way can remove the undisciplined commander from the very site of operations, either by taking him away with him or by some other similar measure. If, for instance, a commander, a superior commander, even the supreme commander, should go to the site itself, to the spot, and then personally give an order for the fire to cease, and one of the subordinates would resist this order and would not in fact implement it, that would be actually flagrant disobeyance [as interpreted] and criminal offence and in this event, therefore, he should take a measure which would also imply, in fact, depriving him of his liberty, and such a potential offender would therefore be turned over to the prosecuting authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would the operational group commander, if obligated to meet with his superior commander at a point later in the day, would that operational group commander be excused from that type of personal intervention required by the continuing pacts which are not being stopped pursuant to orders? Let me make it quite clear: If the operational group commander has to see his superior commander, and yet the activity which is the subject matter of that meeting persists at a very dangerous level, would the operational group commander appropriately seek to defer the meeting and personally intervene in the situation at hand?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, such an assumption that you have just presented obviously is very serious and places the commander in a situation where he has to weigh and assess whether to respond to the requirement of his superior and come and see him, leave his post and go and see him, while, for instance, the situation with his unit critically asks for his personal presence. Well, in this event, obviously, it seems quite normal to me that such a commander, together with his superiors, should judge and assess what is better. Because to stop violation, violation of cease-fire, would be equally important and in the equal interest also of his own superior. Therefore, to defer such a meeting for an hour or two is probably less important than, in fact, stopping the -- than the stoppage of cease-fire. And such a requirement and this need for personal presence obviously still implies and is within the great responsibility of the operational commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness didn't say commander of the operational group. He said operational commander. And these are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when I pose to you, when I speak about the operational group commander, I wish to clarify that I am referring to the commander of the operational group. Is that the same level of officer you are referring to in your response, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, myself, I was actually -- what I had in mind was the commander of the operational group. But this commander is also the commander of VPS. However, both are facing -- both have this dilemma. They have to resolve it, both with their superior. And the same would be also in the case of the commander of the VPS, because he too would have to resolve such a dilemma. But at any rate, he would have to assume responsibility for not having intervened and put an end to the attack because he went to see the -- his superior. To me this cannot be compared.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have been advised that there is a transcript correction, page 76, line 16 should read "cease-fire violation." I think it might be off my screen. Yeah. And then stoppage of cease-fire violation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ultimately, who is -- which commander is ultimately responsible for making sure that the situation is brought under hand? What is the highest level of responsibility? Who is the ultimately responsible officer, commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Within the operations that a given commander in fact leads, well, in the case of the operational group, that is the commander of the operational group, because he is in fact the highest instance -- he has the highest responsibility in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm talking about at the operational level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, allow the witness to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to make sure my question was correct -- was clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the operational group on the operational level, who ultimately bears the responsibility for making sure that the matter at hand is dealt with?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, by all means, the commanding officers [as interpreted] of operational group, because he indeed is the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I believe the transcript says "commanding officers." Did you mean "commanding officer"?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or commander -- let us get our -- let us get our -- commander, commander. We have -- make our term -- commander of the operational group. Thank you. Let us now take the scenario where, hours later, a cease-fire is in fact -- well, fire stops and there is an assessment, there is a report from the other side of serious damage to protected -- sites which are protected under international humanitarian law, as well as to -- injury to civilians in -- within that area, which is also a protected area. Let us talk now about what must -- what steps must be done to react to the information that there has been what, on its face, may be a criminal violation of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the situation after, after the attacks, when the damage has already occurred. Well, in such a case, the commanding officers in the chain of command and the military leadership, as -- in general, have the responsibility to carry -- to bring up the responsibility of those members of the armed officers [as interpreted] who, in fact, participated in the illegal attacks on the unprotected civilian targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do you -- excuse me. I want to clarify. Do you mean -- when you say "unprotected civilian targets," I'm not clear. That's how the translation came out. Would you indicate --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: [In English] Protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This responsibility evidently is a criminal responsibility, because this is a criminal offence, because in fact such attacks on cultural -- on protected cultural monuments is a criminal offence; and the perpetrator, once identified, has to be brought to the military court. Another aspect which, in fact, then remains to be taken into consideration for the commanding officers -- officer and the competent authorities is to ensure that something similar does not happen again; and for it, other measures are called for, are necessary, and to my mind, especially, in fact, measures relating to the personnel. Commanders who are capable of such offences should be removed from their posts, and others -- and they should be replaced by other people who will respect, actually, regulations and orders. With the same people, well, you cannot actually expect that something like it will not happen again with the same people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we discuss what you're referring to as the removal, the process of removal? How does that come about? How is an officer -- or what role does a commander have in the process of removal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, removal of individual commanding officer from their post can be accomplished by a number of ways. One of the ways is, very briefly, issuing of orders by the competent senior officer on removal and transferring of the officer to another post. No disciplinary measure is necessary. This is regular staff measure taken. Another way to remove such an officer from their post is by initiating a criminal procedure against such a person, and the competent investigating judge apprehends them by depriving them of liberty. Similarly, according to the law, it is possible to remove, temporarily remove, an officer from his post if a procedure is initiated against him, in view of a disciplinary infringement, if a disciplinary investigation is initiated against him. Once the disciplinary procedure to court-martial such a person is initiated, then such an officer can be removed from his post. These are some essential ways and means to remove him or her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the first option you mentioned about no disciplinary measures, just a transfer, would that -- did you intend to mean that in the situation where serious criminal violations have occurred, that that is an option, where serious criminal violations such the ones we have just discussed occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, if a criminal offence occurred, then the primary way is to deprive him of liberty and initiate a criminal procedure against him. I've noted a general option that the system of command and control has at its disposal to somebody that has only threatened to use force can be removed from a sensitive post. However, if and when a criminal offence occurred, then the criminal procedure had to be initiated. Thus, the person is removed from his post by competent bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The initiation of the criminal offence, can you indicate how that would come about under these circumstances? I'm sorry. Excuse me. I'm sorry, General. Not the initiation of the criminal offence; initiation of the criminal procedure concerning the offence. I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: It is initiated in the circumstances when it is established that an assumed criminal offence has occurred. If, in a combat situation, during fire, there is no doubt that the criminal offence has occurred, then a military prosecutor must be notified, as well as investigating judge should have been notified, so as to take decision how to proceed. If a commander commanding -- operationally commanding, firing, and if fire still goes on, then he can be deprived of his liberty, also by a competent body of a security service, competent body of military police, or his superior officer, who is on a higher-ranking level than him. All these could deprive him of liberty until investigating judge decides on how to proceed, and then investigating judge takes over the criminal procedure against this particular person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the commander of the operational group, as the highest commanding officer in that group, have an obligation to ensure that the information about the violations, about the criminal violations, reaches the appropriate prosecuting or criminally investigating authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: All levels of commanding posts must or shall provide for that. If this is not provided for on a lower level, then the commander leading such an operation is the superior officer and the most responsible to provide for this matter. And when this is done, the military prosecutor is notified. But this does not imply that he personally must notify the military prosecutor. He personally must check and verify whether the military police has been informed, whether the military police has notified the prosecutor, whether other subordinate officers have done so. If that has been done, it has been implemented, and his responsibility is that, in one way or another, the prosecutor has been notified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This applies to the commander of the operational group, that he must personally check and verify whether the military police have been informed, whether they've notified the prosecutor, whether other subordinate officers have done so? Is this what you are saying is the obligation of the commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Well, the commander of such a level as operative group has its own command. In this command, he has his own body, an assistant for political and legal matters. He has a legal clerk. He also has a head of security service, or any body can acquire information and check the information and just notify the commander on the result. Prosecutor's office is notified, then commander can say "thanks." Or prosecutor's office has not been notified, he can command anybody in his staff that this be done, thus providing for the initiation of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander of the operational group is aware of the allegations of the crime having been committed. There appears to be no action taken by a military prosecutor. Nothing seems to be happening. Is there -- what is the obligation of the commander of the operational group to ensure that, in fact, because he knows the allegations have been lodged, to, in fact, that information reaches the military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: The interest and the responsibility of the commander is that the procedure is initiated, and that is duly carried out. However, if this has not happened, in view of something has occurred with the investigating judge or the prosecutor - of course, we are now speaking in terms of the implementation of criminal responsibility for what has happened for illegal firing - he then must notify his superior, and namely that no measures have been taken by the judicial bodies. For example, in view of the questions as you have already put to me, if, for example, the competent investigating judge or military prosecutors get killed, in such a case, commander notifies his superiors, and the superior then notifies other high-ranking bodies to guarantee for the replacement of lower judicial bodies, that cannot carry out their duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you more specifically: If it becomes apparent that the other persons within the operational group who could communicate the information, either through the military police or by some other means, to the military prosecutor, have not done so, have not done so, not because of death or whatever of the military prosecutor, then what is the obligation, the responsibility, of the commander of the operational group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: His responsibility is to make sure that this data reaches the military prosecutor. If none of his subordinates or others have done so, then he must demand for this to be done by somebody else. Or similar, he may also demand this from commanders from his own command on the level of operational group, which is all possible. If there is no communication with prosecutor's office, the commander can then ask that this be communicated through his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he must -- do I understand you correctly: But he must ensure that the information is communicated? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN ZORC
utterances.text: Right. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I note that it is 4.00. I assume the next question to me will be: How much longer. If I may examine respectfully for part of the morning session, less one hour, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. [Microphone not activated] I must adjourn for the evening now. We will resume again at 9.00 in the morning and your evidence will continue then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
